The marginal “Mais il faut supposer … que $\Gamma_X$ est de dim … finie !” qualifies the unrestricted global hyper-Tor construction, while another note treats a bounded-below second argument for derived internal Hom. ### N08. Finite coefficient rings force attention to unbounded resolutions

The warning that $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is not a field and need not have finite global Tor dimension explains the move from degree-zero sheaves into $D^-$, while 112 emphasizes that tensor and derived Hom can have unbounded cohomological effects even at a geometric point. The opening remark on 108 explicitly leaves finite-Tor and finite-Ext refinements outside the current scope. This is a methodological precursor to the perfect-complex trace construction on 130–146, not evidence that all finite coefficient modules are perfect. The literal warning about $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ also needs arithmetic scope: squarefree $n$ gives a product of fields, whereas $n=\ell^2$ gives the actual obstruction checked in N10.

A concrete check of “même si $X$ … un pt géométrique” is $A=\mathbb Z/\ell^2\mathbb Z$ and $M=A/\ell A$: the resolution with every differential multiplication by $\ell$ is exact, while tensoring it with $M$ makes every differential zero. Hence $\operatorname{Tor}_i^A(M,M)\cong M$ for every $i\geq0$, so locally constant finite modules do not automatically give bounded derived tensor products. This is our elementary example, adding an explicit witness to the manuscript's warning, not a claim that the example is written there.

On 132, “L'existence … se ramène à prouver” invariance under isomorphism is an unfinished reduction at the page boundary; 134 continues it by vanishing on acyclic bounded finite-projective complexes and short exact sequences. It is therefore a proof sketch completed in these pages, not an indefinitely abandoned existence claim. The corresponding independence-of-representative statement is verified in The Stacks Project Authors (n.d., [Tag 03TI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03TI)); the manuscript's contribution to the supplied plan is its explicit passage from an alternating expression to a derived invariant.

The manuscript uses one fixed interval for “tout pt géom,” a quantifier that should be retained in any reconstruction. On a disjoint union of infinitely many points, put a copy of $A$ in cohomological degree $-n$ on the $n$th component: this is locally perfect and bounded above, with finite Tor-amplitude at every stalk, but it has no single global finite amplitude interval. The example distinguishes the manuscript's uniform claim from the local perfectness criterion (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 08G8](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/08G8)); it does not refute the fixed-interval stalkwise criterion on the page.

### N25. A perfect complex with nonprojective cohomology

Let $A=\mathbb Z/\ell^2\mathbb Z$ and take the two-term complex $P=[A\xrightarrow{\ell}A]$ in degrees $0,1$. It is perfect, with $H^0(P)\cong H^1(P)\cong A/\ell A$ nonprojective, while the trace of its identity is unambiguously $1-1=0$ in $A$ by the finite-projective supertrace formula (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 03TI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03TI)). This gives a concrete reason for the manuscript's replacement of the system of cohomology groups by its complex, and differs from N10 because the **object** here is perfect even though its cohomology modules are not.

### N25. A perfect complex with nonprojective cohomology

Let $A=\mathbb Z/\ell^2\mathbb Z$ and take the two-term complex $P=[A\xrightarrow{\ell}A]$ in degrees $0,1$. It is perfect, with $H^0(P)\cong H^1(P)\cong A/\ell A$ nonprojective, while the trace of its identity is unambiguously $1-1=0$ in $A$ by the finite-projective supertrace formula (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., [Tag 03TI](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03TI)). This gives a concrete reason for the manuscript's replacement of the system of cohomology groups by its complex, and differs from N10 because the **object** here is perfect even though its cohomology modules are not.
